en: Data poisoning is yet another term that's
interesting to know when talking about model
training and post-training.
The idea is that you, of course, don't have
to feed
useful or reasonable data into an AI model.
You
don't have to train a model to behave in a
good way. Instead, you could feed data into
a model to
get it to extract and steal data from the
system it's running on or from the users
that are using it, for example,
or to be unfriendly, to have a simpler
example. So data poisoning is all about
feeding
bad data into the training process. Now, the
poisoning part is that this typically does
not happen deliberately, but instead
you could be publishing a lot of articles on
the internet, the World Wide Web, that
include examples of behaviors that are not
good. And you could hope that that data gets
picked up in the next training run of a top
model
and influences that model to behave in a way
you don't want it to behave.
It's kind of a made-up example, but it can
happen. It can especially happen on a lower
scale if we're talking about fine-tuning and
you have a way of sneaking data into the
fine-tuning data of a company. Let's say
an unhappy employee who knows that their
company is running a fine-tuning process and
wants to take revenge and sneaks some data
in there that gets the model to
send all the data it later operates on via
email to the competitors of the company.
That would be data poisoning.
